title: Master Level Analysis of My Games at US Chess Open!!! | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: A must-win game against a strong junior. I take the mainline Open Sicilian with the knight to f3, and he steers toward his pet setup.
He answers e6 — the flexible move-order that keeps both the Kan and the Taimanov on the table.
Earlier in the event I met this with c3, the Alapin, and won a nice game — but he'll have spent the break preparing exactly that.
So I switch it up and open the position with d4, the Open Sicilian, to sidestep his prep.
After the trades on d4 he plays the Kan with a6, staking out the queenside and denying my pieces the b5-square.
teaches: Kan: ...a6 controls b5 and prepares queenside expansion

moves.spoken: I develop the bishop to d3 — the main line, aiming it straight at his kingside.
He comes out with the bishop to c5, pressuring my centralized knight.
I nudge the knight back to b3, and he tucks the bishop onto a7, where it eyes the long diagonal and becomes his best piece.
teaches: The a7-bishop is Black\u2019s pride in this structure

moves.spoken: There's a known plan here of Qg4, provoking a kingside weakness before dropping back to e2. White is judged a touch better, but it's rich and double-edged. My idea was Qe2 followed by Be3 to trade off that strong dark-squared bishop — and, going for broke, the engine's wild suggestion of castling queenside.
plans: Qg4 to provoke a kingside weakness
Qe2 and Be3 to neutralize the dark-squared bishop
Consider long castling for a sharp fight
